articles.title: Vụ nhìn thấy UFO đáng tin cậy nhất trong lịch sử: Hé lộ bí mật về UFO tại Thổ Nhĩ Kỳ
articles.text:
Đã nhiều năm trôi qua kể từ khi sự cố UFO của Thổ Nhĩ Kỳ xảy ra và nhiều manh mối liên quan vẫn chưa được xác minh.
Việc nhìn thấy UFO xảy ra thường xuyên trên khắp thế giới, mặc dù hầu hết mọi người chưa từng chứng kiến những hiện tượng bí ẩn này nhưng chúng vẫn là một trong những bí ẩn chưa có lời giải của nhân loại. Trong số những trường hợp nhìn thấy UFO này, video rõ ràng nhất về UFO được một người đàn ông Thổ Nhĩ Kỳ tên Yalcin Yalman quay vào năm 2008.
Đoạn video đã gây náo động ngay khi được tung ra, thậm chí còn trở thành bằng chứng chắc chắn được những người đam mê UFO sử dụng để chứng minh sự tồn tại của nền văn minh ngoài Trái đất. Đây cũng là video UFO đầu tiên được chứng nhận là không thể giả mạo.
Thậm chí, có người còn sử dụng phân tích kỹ thuật để phát hiện ra rằng có người ngoài hành tinh di chuyển xung quanh UFO. Đây có phải là bằng chứng thực sự chắc chắn về sự tồn tại của nền văn minh ngoài Trái đất? Trong bài viết này, chúng ta sẽ nói về những vụ nhìn thấy UFO nổi tiếng của Thổ Nhĩ Kỳ.
UFO xuất hiện tại Thổ Nhĩ Kỳ năm 2008. (Ảnh minh họa: Metabunk).
Vào năm 2008, một số hiện tượng kỳ lạ xảy ra trên bầu trời Thổ Nhĩ Kỳ, người dân nhiều thành phố đã chứng kiến những hiện tượng không giải thích được. Những UFO này lóe lên ánh sáng chói lóa, lặng lẽ bay lượn trên biển và xuất hiện mà không có bất kỳ âm thanh nào.
Ban đầu mọi người không quá để ý đến điều này mà cho rằng có thể đó chỉ là ảo ảnh do bóng bay hoặc ánh đèn gây ra. Tuy nhiên, với sự xuất hiện thường xuyên của UFO, con người bắt đầu cảm thấy tò mò và sợ hãi, dần dần họ nhận ra rằng những chiếc máy bay bí ẩn này không phải là vật bình thường.
Đúng lúc mọi người đang bàn tán thì một người đàn ông trung niên tên Yalcin Yalman đã quay một đoạn video khiến cả thế giới chấn động. Đó là một buổi sáng sớm tháng 6 năm 2008, Yalcin Yalman tình cờ chứng kiến một điểm sáng trên bầu trời và anh tò mò ghi lại nó bằng máy ảnh DV của mình. Khi phóng to bức ảnh, anh vô cùng sốc khi phát hiện điểm sáng không phải là ánh sáng hay ngôi sao mà là một chiếc máy bay màu bạc hình đĩa.
Điểm sáng không phải là ánh sáng hay ngôi sao mà là một chiếc máy bay màu bạc hình đĩa. (Ảnh minh họa: Metabunk)
Chiếc máy bay này không có đặc điểm gì giống với máy bay hiện đại, nó lặng lẽ trôi trên biển mà không gây ra bất kỳ âm thanh nào. Điều đáng ngạc nhiên hơn nữa là từ khoảng trống ở giữa máy bay, có thể nhìn thấy hai sinh vật hình người đang di chuyển bên trong. Yalcin Yalman cảm thấy mình đã ghi lại được một khám phá lớn nên đã gửi đoạn video ghi lại được đến Trung tâm Nghiên cứu Khoa học Vũ trụ UFO.
Trung tâm nghiên cứu này là một tổ chức chuyên nghiên cứu về việc nhìn thấy UFO. Các chuyên gia tại trung tâm nghiên cứu tin rằng đoạn video này là một trong những hình ảnh UFO rõ ràng và quan trọng nhất từng được ghi lại.
So với các bằng chứng nhìn thấy UFO khác, đường nét và chi tiết của UFO trong video này rất rõ ràng và ấn tượng. Từ quan điểm bề ngoài, UFO này không phù hợp với bất kỳ máy bay nào được nhân loại biết đến. Sau nhiều lần cân nhắc kỹ lưỡng bởi các nhân viên của trung tâm nghiên cứu, họ quyết định công khai dữ liệu hình ảnh này.
Đường nét và chi tiết của UFO trong video này rất rõ ràng và ấn tượng. (Ảnh minh họa: Metabunk).
Thế là đài truyền hình Thổ Nhĩ Kỳ lần đầu tiên tung ra một video clip gây ấn tượng mạnh, được cho là video rõ nét nhất về UFO trong lịch sử. Đoạn video dài 2 phút 30 giây này ngay lập tức gây xôn xao dư luận và gây tranh cãi.
Hầu như tất cả mọi người đều nghi ngờ rằng đây là một trò lừa đảo của đài truyền hình Thổ Nhĩ Kỳ, họ cho rằng tài liệu video là giả mạo và chỉ là những hiệu ứng được sản xuất bằng phần mềm hoặc công nghệ hiệu ứng đặc biệt. Vụ việc nhanh chóng gây ra một cuộc tranh luận sôi nổi giữa những người đam mê UFO và những người ủng hộ khoa học, cả hai bên đều nhất quyết giữ quan điểm riêng của mình và không chịu thỏa hiệp.
Tuy nhiên, trước sự kiên quyết của nhà nghiên cứu Akdogan, những dữ liệu hình ảnh này đã được gửi đến Hội đồng Khoa học và Công nghệ Thổ Nhĩ Kỳ và Đài quan sát Thiên văn Quốc gia để phân tích sơ bộ.
Cả hai tổ chức đều là tổ chức chính thức của Thổ Nhĩ Kỳ và quy tụ các chuyên gia hàng đầu về vật lý, thiên văn học và các lĩnh vực khác. Ban đầu, mục đích của các nhà nghiên cứu là tìm ra bằng chứng về việc Yalman giả mạo video từ đoạn video gốc dài 22 phút.
Video là thật và không có dấu vết lừa đảo. (Ảnh minh họa: Metabunk)
Tuy nhiên, điều đáng kinh ngạc hơn nữa là sau khi quan sát cẩn thận, các chuyên gia không thể tìm thấy bất kỳ dấu vết nào của việc sản xuất hiệu ứng đặc biệt. Kết luận này buộc các nhà nghiên cứu phải thừa nhận rằng không có nghi ngờ gì về tính xác thực của đoạn video.
Không chỉ vậy, các chuyên gia video và các công ty hiệu ứng đặc biệt đến từ Nhật Bản, Nga và Mỹ cũng xác định và đưa ra kết luận tương tự: video là thật và không có dấu vết lừa đảo.
Điều này càng làm sâu sắc thêm bí ẩn về việc nhìn thấy UFO này và mọi người bắt đầu tự hỏi, liệu đây có thực sự là tàu vũ trụ của một nền văn minh ngoài Trái đất? Mặc dù video này đã được nhiều chuyên gia ủng hộ và công nhận nhưng một số người cũng đưa ra những ý kiến và nghi ngờ khác nhau về nó.
Những người này cho rằng UFO trong video chỉ là hình ảnh từ nóc tàu du lịch hoặc ảo ảnh, còn những sinh vật bên trong chỉ là hình chiếu của khách du lịch hoặc vật thể khác. Họ tin rằng đây là những hiện tượng quang học hoặc ảo ảnh quang học và không có gì huyền bí về chúng.
Nhiều người cho rằng UFO là hình ảnh từ nóc tàu du lịch hoặc ảo ảnh. (Ảnh minh họa: Metabunk).
Nguyên nhân chính của những người này là do thời gian và địa điểm quay video trùng với lộ trình đi thuyền và lịch trình của một số tàu du lịch địa phương, tàu vũ trụ trong video có thể là đèn hoặc đồ trang trí trên đầu tàu du lịch. Điều kiện quay video không tốt, có các yếu tố gây nhiễu như sương mù, hơi nước, ánh sáng, tàu vũ trụ trong video có thể là ảo ảnh hoặc hiện tượng khúc xạ khí quyển. Góc và khoảng cách quay video không lý tưởng, có các vấn đề như ảo ảnh thị giác, biến dạng, và các sinh vật trong video có thể là hình chiếu hoặc hình ảnh phản chiếu của khách du lịch hoặc các vật thể khác trên cửa sổ.
Tuy nhiên, những lý do này không được hỗ trợ bởi bằng chứng thuyết phục và chúng không thể giải thích tại sao UFO này có thể xuất hiện ở cùng một nơi trong nhiều tháng liên tục mà không bị radar phát hiện.
Hơn nữa, những lý do này không thể giải thích tại sao tàu vũ trụ và các sinh vật trong video lại có nhiều điểm tương đồng với UFO và người ngoài hành tinh được các nhân chứng khác mô tả. Vì vậy, những lý do này không thể phủ nhận tính chân thực và tầm quan trọng của đoạn video, cũng như không thể phủ nhận sự tồn tại và liên hệ của các nền văn minh ngoài Trái đất.
Chủ đề về UFO luôn là chủ đề bị ảnh hưởng nặng nề nhất bởi những tin đồn. (Ảnh minh họa: Metabunk).
Đã nhiều năm trôi qua kể từ khi sự cố UFO của Thổ Nhĩ Kỳ xảy ra và nhiều manh mối liên quan vẫn chưa được xác minh. Ngay cả với những minh chứng và đánh giá chính thức của các chuyên gia từ nhiều quốc gia khác nhau thì vẫn còn nhiều điều không chắc chắn.
Theo những định nghĩa hiện tại, UFO dùng để chỉ vật thể bay không xác định, tức là tất cả vật thể bay không thể xác định và xác minh nguồn gốc đều có thể gọi là UFO. Tuy nhiên, chủ đề về UFO luôn là chủ đề bị ảnh hưởng nặng nề nhất bởi những tin đồn. Không ai có thể chắc chắn rằng UFO phải là máy bay của người ngoài hành tinh và không ai có thể chứng minh liệu người ngoài hành tinh có tồn tại hay không.

articles.title: Hồ nước đỏ như máu ở Tanzania này sở hữu siêu năng lực biến hầu hết các sinh vật thành đá
articles.text:
Nước hồ Natron có màu đỏ như máu, đặc điểm này càng nổi bật ở những nơi có tỷ lệ bốc hơi cao.
Hồ Natron là một hồ nước muối nằm ở phía Bắc Tanzania, phía Đông Bắc miệng núi lửa Ngorongoro và gần biên giới Kenya. Ẩn mình giữa những ngọn núi lửa, hồ Natron nằm tại điểm thấp nhất của thung lũng Great Rift với độ cao 600m so với mực nước biển.
Hồ Natron
Hồ được cung cấp nước từ sông Southern Ewaso Ng'iro và những suối nước nóng giàu khoáng chất. Nước hồ khá nông, sâu chưa đầy 3m và chiều rộng của nó thay đổi tùy thuộc vào mực nước. Trong khi đó, mực nước trong hồ lại thường xuyên thay đổi do hồ có mức độ bốc hơi cao, khiến các loại muối và khoáng chất, đặc biệt là natri cacbonat (natron) tập trung dưới lòng hồ. Khu vực xung quanh hồ rất khô nóng và bụi bặm, không thuận lợi cho những chuyến du lịch.
Nếu đến thăm Natron, du khách sẽ được thưởng thức một trong những cảnh quan độc đáo nhất ở Tanzania. Nước hồ Natron có màu đỏ như máu, đặc điểm này càng nổi bật ở những nơi có tỷ lệ bốc hơi cao. Khi nước bốc hơi vào mùa khô, độ mặn tăng đến mức các vi sinh vật ưa mặn cũng bắt đầu phát triển. Chủng vi sinh vật này đã tạo nên sắc đỏ đậm của nước hồ, ở những nơi cạn hơn, nước hồ có màu da cam.
Nhiệt độ khá cao (khoảng 41 độ C) cùng với hàm lượng muối cao, không đồng đều trong hồ khiến Natron không phải là môi trường sống thuận lợi cho các loài động vật hoang dã.
Mặc dù hầu hết các sinh vật không thể uống nước hồ nóng, nhưng đó lại là một môi trường hoàn hảo cho một vi sinh vật ưa mặn được gọi là vi khuẩn lam. Nó cũng là nguyên nhân làm cho hồ có màu đỏ - các sắc tố quang hợp trong vi khuẩn lam có màu đỏ khi ở các phần sâu của nước, trong khi các phần nông của hồ có màu đỏ cam hơn.
Hồ nước này còn được mệnh danh là "hồ tử thần" do từ hàng nghìn năm nay, bất kỳ loài vật nào sảy chân ngã xuống hồ, xác của chúng đều bị hóa đá trong một thời gian ngắn. "Thủ phạm" gây ra hiện tượng kỳ lạ trên tại hồ Natron là ngọn núi lửa một triệu năm tuổi, có tên gọi Ol Doinyo Lengai, nằm ở phía Nam hồ Natron. Dung nham từ ngọn núi chảy xuống mang theo lượng muối khoáng đặc biệt.
Thực tế, hồ Natron là một hồ nước tù.
Mặc dù bề mặt đầy màu sắc này có thể rất quyến rũ trong mắt của nhiều người, nhưng đó là một cái bẫy chết người đối với hầu hết các loài động vật. Nước kiềm của hồ Natron có thể đạt đến mức độ pH cao tới 12, trong khi điều kiện phù hợp với sự sống thường chỉ ở mức độ pH gần 7. Và nếu bạn xuống tắm ở hồ này, các hóa chất trong nước sẽ đốt cháy da và mắt của bạn. Nếu một sinh vật uống nước, nó rất có thể sẽ chết do bị tổn thương nặng ở cấp độ tế bào, hệ thần kinh và gan.
Trên thực tế, hồ Natron là một hồ nước tù, nước chỉ có thể bốc hơi mà không có sự trao đổi với bên ngoài. Nước hồ có một chất hóa học có tên là Natron - hỗn hợp với thành phần chính là Natri Bicacbonat (NaHCO3) và Natri Cacbonat (Na2CO3). Chất này đi vào hồ thông qua các vật chất xói mòn từ các ngọn đồi xung quanh. Do không thể thoát đi mà cứ bốc hơi nên nước trong hồ có nồng độ kiềm rất cao.
Điều đó nói rằng, không ai thực sự biết chắc chắn chính xác cách thức các loài động vật chết sau khi uống phải nước của hồ này.
Do đặc điểm riêng biệt của hồ, động vật chết trong nước đều bị vôi hóa. Người ta thường nói rằng hồ Natron có thể biến những con vật kém may mắn này thành đá, nhưng trên thực tế, nó giống như một quá trình ướp xác hơn.

articles.title: Neanderthal DNA still survives in our human family tree. What were our ancient relatives' relationships like?
articles.text:
Neanderthal DNA still survives in our human family tree. What were our ancient relatives' relationships like?
Developing research suggests that ancient interbreeding wasn't random — it was socially patterned, directional and far more complicated than the headlines suggest.
Deep in a limestone cave on Turkey's Mediterranean coast, two very different sets of humans left behind nearly identical traces of their lives — similar stone tools, the remains of the same prey animals, the same types of seashells pierced and strung into ornaments. They may have been separated by thousands of years and may not have directly interacted. Yet the overlap between them was striking enough that researchers studying the site had to look twice.
The site, Üçağızlı II, offers one of the clearest examples of a conundrum that scientists have long wrestled with: Neanderthals and modern humans (Homo sapiens) didn't just collide and go their separate ways. They inhabited the same areas, and, as dozens of genetic studies have confirmed, had sex, across tens of thousands of years and on multiple continents. The DNA of nearly every person alive outside Africa today carries the proof: Roughly 2% of the non-African genome is Neanderthal.
And yet, there is not a single archaeological site that shows them living together. Knowing that modern humans and Neanderthals mated is not the same as understanding how it happened. Who approached whom? Were these interactions consensual? Were they the result of violence or trade alliances? Who raised these hybrid babies? And what does the genetic record tell us about the social lives of two different kinds of humans navigating each other's existence for the first time?
Some of the answers, it turns out, are written on the X chromosome — and they are stranger than expected.
A puzzle on the X chromosome
The first high-coverage Neanderthal genome was sequenced in 2010, and for the next 15 years, researchers kept noticing something puzzling: Neanderthal DNA was less common from the X chromosomes in people alive today.
One of the two sex chromosomes in humans, the X chromosome represents about 5% of the DNA in cells. Most females carry a pair of X chromosomes in each cell, while most males have one X and one Y.
Everywhere else in our genome, traces of long-ago breeding between Neanderthals and modern humans showed up in roughly consistent proportions. But on the X chromosome, there was far less Neanderthal DNA.
The leading explanation was negative selection — the idea that Neanderthal gene variants unique to the X chromosome were somehow incompatible with modern-human biology and had been gradually eliminated from the gene pool over thousands of generations. It was a reasonable hypothesis, given that incompatibilities elsewhere in the genome did lead to the weeding out of Neanderthal DNA on other chromosomes over time.
To understand why negative selection explanation didn't explain the X chromosome data, however, it helps to know what different parts of the genome actually do. Some stretches of DNA are protein-coding regions; they contain the instructions for building proteins, the molecular machinery that does most of the work inside cells. Others are regulatory sequences that don't build proteins themselves but help control when and how much of a protein gets produced. And then there are still other stretches of DNA that don’t appear to code for proteins or directly regulate gene expression, though researchers suspect at least some have functions we don’t yet fully understand.
Alexander Platt, an evolutionary biologist at the University of Pennsylvania's Perelman School of Medicine, hypothesized that if the problem was that Neanderthal gene variants on the X chromosome were inherently harmful, modern-human X gene variants would have been advantageous in Neanderthals. As a result, X chromosomal DNA extracted from Neanderthal skeletons should show an excess of modern-human DNA in stretches of the genome where they'd provide measurable benefit. They reasoned that this excess would likely appear in protein-coding genes or the regulatory regions that control their expression, not noncoding DNA.
But that's not what they found. Instead, Neanderthal X chromosomes carried more modern-human DNA in the noncoding regions of the genome than in coding regions. This pattern didn't reflect selection for better gene variants. It was a signature of reproduction — a record of who was passing chromosomes to whom.
In a typical pregnancy, the mother contributes an X chromosome via the egg, and the father contributes either an X or a Y via the sperm cell. So, while an individual is guaranteed to inherit their mother's X, they don't necessarily carry their father's — males exclusively inherit their mother's X. That pattern differs from the other 22 pairs of chromosomes, which mothers and fathers contribute to equally. Across a population, then, two-thirds of X chromosomes are inherited from mothers and one-third from fathers.
This fact makes the X chromosome a particularly sensitive recorder of who was reproducing with whom.
Long-standing sexual preference
Tracking the flow of X chromosomes can reveal trends in Neanderthal-human mating. If Neanderthal males paired with modern-human females more often than Neanderthal females paired with modern-human males, you'd see more modern-human X chromosomes flow into the Neanderthal gene pool.
When the team ran simulations to explore this idea, the data suggested what Platt described as a persistent, recurring mating preference: Males with more Neanderthal ancestry tended to reproduce with females with more modern-human ancestry. And this trend held across at least two distinct mating periods separated by around 200,000 years, said Platt.
This finding gave the researchers a new window into the timeline of mating between Neanderthals and modern humans. Platt's team identified at least two distinct pulses: one roughly 45,000 years ago, which produced the majority the Neanderthal DNA that lives on in non-African genomes today, and an earlier period over 200,000 years ago, whose genetic traces survived not in modern-human populations but in Neanderthals.
The pattern of Neanderthal males having offspring with H. sapiens females appears in both periods, separated by more than 150,000 years.
What the X chromosome data alone cannot say is why the pattern exists. It documents who reproduced with whom. It says nothing about who wanted whom.
Biological incompatibility
That distinction matters, because the same genetic signature can emerge from very different causes, and some have nothing to do with sexual preference.
Rajiv McCoy, a geneticist at Johns Hopkins University, pointed out that biology alone could produce a genetic signal like this one. When closely related species interbreed, the success of a pregnancy can depend not just on whose genes are inherited but on which parent belongs to which group.
Even if Neanderthal genes work fine in a modern-human genetic background, hybrid pregnancies may simply have been more likely to succeed when the Neanderthal was the father rather than the mother. That's not because of either parent's sexual preferences, but because of how their respective biologies interacted in the womb, McCoy told Live Science.
Researchers have recently proposed a few mechanisms that fit neatly with this theory. One study suggests that Neanderthal red blood cells restricted fetuses' growth in the womb. Another proposed that Neanderthal mothers carrying hybrid offspring may have been more prone to preeclampsia, a life-threatening pregnancy complication. Nothing in the existing data definitively rules such causes, McCoy said.
In practice, the two explanations are hard to separate. "Our models have no way of distinguishing mating from mating that produces a viable and fertile offspring," McCoy said. If hybrid pregnancies failed more often when the mother was Neanderthal, the genetic record would look similar to a world where Neanderthal females mated less often with H. sapiens males. Sexual encounters that didn't result in offspring left no genetic trace.
For now, the question of what drove that bias — social preference, or biology — remains open. Whatever barriers existed between the groups, they clearly weren't absolute. Multiple distinct episodes of interbreeding over thousands of years, McCoy noted, is itself evidence that the fertility of hybrid individuals was "sufficiently intact to leave a lasting mark."
How Neanderthal and human groups interacted
Bridget Alex, a researcher in human evolutionary biology at Harvard University who has spent her career reconstructing the timing and geography of Neanderthal-H. sapiens overlap, cautioned that all this is hampered by one fact: no direct archaeological evidence reveals how the two groups interacted.
"Despite a century and a half of Neanderthal research," she told Live Science, "no one's ever found a Neanderthal and Homo sapiens fossil in the same exact layer dated to the same exact period at the same exact site."
Instead, we have a regional and variable patchwork shaped by conditions that shifted over thousands of years and hundreds to thousands of miles.
Neanderthals inhabited a territory stretching from Siberia to Iberia to Southwest Asia between roughly 250,000 and 40,000 years ago. Modern humans were evolving in Africa during much of that span and came out repeatedly, in multiple waves, meeting Neanderthals in different times and places, with likely very different outcomes each time, Alex said.
"It's not like the Neanderthals living in what's now Spain could call up the ones in what's now Uzbekistan and be like, 'OK, what's our policy with modern humans? Do we kill them, have sex with them, ignore them?'" she said. "My assumption has always been that interactions would vary across time and space depending on the particular environmental conditions, social conditions, and just the whims of a particular group."
At Grotte Mandrin, a cave in the Rhône Valley in southern France, archaeologists found one of the most illuminating records of what those encounters may have looked like. Ludovic Slimak, a paleoanthropologist at the University of Toulouse who has spent years excavating the site, described it as something genetics alone can't offer: "an extraordinarily precise archaeological sequence of Neanderthals and [Homo] sapiens occupying exactly the same place," he told Live Science in an email.
Neanderthal artifacts fill layer after layer of radiocarbon and luminescence dating up to about 57,000 years ago. And then, in one thin layer dated to between 56,800 and 51,700 years ago, there's a set of different stone tools and a single tooth that appear to belong to H. sapiens. Then, in layers immediately above, beginning around 51,700 years ago, Neanderthal artifacts appear again. That group of modern humans arrived, lived briefly in a continent otherwise inhabited entirely by Neanderthals, and then disappeared.
"What strikes me most is not mixture but proximity without fusion," Slimak told Live Science in an email. In other words, the two groups left no trace of cultural exchange or shared practice.There were "two human populations occupying the same landscape, probably encountering one another, while remaining culturally and biologically very different," Slimak said.
Genetics also paints a portrait of two very different social architectures. Two sites exemplify the trends: At Sunghir, a burial site in Russia dating to around 34,000 years ago, two H. sapiens adolescents were interred head to head beneath thousands of ivory beads and mammoth-bone spears. Ancient DNA analysis showed they were not immediate family members, yet they were buried together in an elaborate ceremony that implies a social world much wider than their immediate group.
In contrast, at Chagyrskaya, a cave site in Siberia, Neanderthals buried in what appears to be a single community layer included a father and his teenage daughter, and a second pair of individuals who shared roughly a quarter of their DNA.
While these are just two sites, they reflect a broader trend that shows up repeatedly in genetic data: Human groups tended to operate through what Alex described as a nested structure: Tens of thousands of years ago, small groups of perhaps 20 or 30 individuals maintained broader ties through ceremonies, intermarriage between human groups and exchange with other groups.
In contrast, data from Neanderthal sites reveal that they tended to cluster in small, tightly knit groups that remained relatively separate from other Neanderthal populations.
Unlike modern humans, Neanderthals didn't regularly mate with individuals in other communities, Alex said. The result, written in their genomes, is that individuals within a single Neanderthal group were often closely related. Their genomes show low genetic diversity across the board, — "kind of suggesting they're always a population on the verge," Alex said, "like an endangered species."
Still, there had to be some out-group mating. At sites where researchers have extracted genomes from several Neanderthal individuals, the pattern is consistent: Male Neanderthals were more closely related to each other than female Neanderthals were to each other. Females, by contrast, seemed more likely to have come from elsewhere. This is the signature of a "patrilocal" social structure in which males stay in their birth groups and females move between them.
Neanderthals' insularity sharpens a key question: If Neanderthal groups weren't regularly folding in Neanderthal females from distant communities, they would probably be even less likely to incorporate female H. sapiens. So how did modern-human women end up producing offspring with Neanderthal men at all?
A numbers problem
Fernando Villanea, a population geneticist at the University of Colorado Boulder, thinks the question may be framed backward. The image of Neanderthal males raising hybrid children with modern-human females within Neanderthal communities, he argues, probably inverts what actually happened.
Something the genomes of late Neanderthals — those living toward the end of their long history in Eurasia — make clear is that they were roughly 10 times more inbred than the modern human ancestors who were then expanding out of Africa in large numbers, he noted. That level of inbreeding isn't usually a choice; it reflects how small and fragmented Neanderthal populations likely were.
Archaeological and paleoclimatic data fill in the context: The ecosystems Neanderthals were best adapted to were shrinking as the planet entered a warmer, more humid period. Modern humans, who had evolved in hotter, wetter African environments, were simply better suited to Europe's new conditions, experts think.
The resulting numerical imbalance changes how scientists think about mating between Neanderthals and modern humans.
"We need to imagine scenarios where a majority of modern human groups traveling into Eurasia are encountering a vanishing minority of Neanderthals," Villanea told Live Science.
In the crucial period between roughly 50,000 and 44,000 years ago, when much of the interbreeding that left a trace in our DNA took place, Neanderthal DNA made up 5% of the modern human genome. Given how heavily humans outnumbered Neanderthals at the time, "that's a lot of matings occurring between the two." The most likely story, Villanea proposes, is "human groups absorbing surviving Neanderthal individuals and raising their children in a mostly human group."
His 2018 study in the journal Nature Ecology & Evolution established that this happened across multiple distinct episodes — and the later ones are particularly telling. Some ancient H. sapiens genomes from Europe around 40,000 years ago, according to the study, carry Neanderthal ancestry from individuals who lived just a few generations after archaeologists can no longer find any physical trace of Neanderthals in the region at all.
Even the very last Neanderthal survivors were still contributing to the H. sapiens gene pool. A 2024 study by Leonardo Iasi and colleagues similarly determined that almost 90% of total Neanderthal ancestry in humans today came from a main pulse roughly 50,000 to 45,000 years ago, likely in the Middle East, with the rest trickling in from more sporadic encounters scattered across Eurasia.
That paints a picture of meetings becoming rarer and rarer as Neanderthals disappeared, with hybridization continuing whenever they did meet up. "This, to me, says deliberate integration of Neanderthal individuals into human groups," Villanea said.
The cost of being hybrid
We know that some hybrid Neanderthal-H. sapiens survived because "we still carry the legacy of their existence," Alex said. However, we know they didn't thrive, because the Neanderthal ancestry our ancestral populations eroded quickly.
Most genes work in concert with other genes across the genome. When Neanderthal-specific variants entered the modern-human genome, it was like trying to put gears from one machine into a slightly different one; the parts didn't quite fit together. As a result, natural selection removed the Neanderthal variants rapidly. Villanea's calculations, based on the rate at which chromosomes recombine during cell division, suggest the drop from the original approximately 5% Neanderthal DNA roughly 50,000 to 45,000 years ago to the roughly 2% carried today happened in around 10 human generations.
"That's very fast," he said. "In real-life terms, that means a lot of hybrids did not survive to reproduce, and the ones that did probably had to deal with life-long health problems."
Platt's team looked at genetic evidence from multiple sites across Eurasia and found that the genetic purge ran in the opposite direction, too. Modern-human DNA was also being selected out of Neanderthal genomes.
Neither had inherently superior genes, Platt concluded. The gene variants were simply optimized for the separate evolutionary histories of their respective lineages, hundreds of thousands of years of independent adaptation that made certain combinations disadvantageous, if not fatal.
Where the hybrids ended up
If Neanderthal males and modern-human females really were producing more surviving offspring than the reverse pairing, where did those children end up?
Villanea was cautious about reading too much into the X chromosome pattern on its own to answer that question. The imbalance Platt found is real, he said — not a statistical quirk. But "there is nothing in the X chromosome data that says it's based on human or Neanderthal mating preference," as Platt proposes.
The same pattern could, in theory, emerge from Neanderthal males leaving their birth groups to find mates, but as archaeological evidence suggests, this was not typical behavior. More likely, he argues, is something biological.
In Peromyscus maniculatus and Peromyscus polionotus — two closely related species of North American deer mouse — a phenomenon called genomic imprinting causes hybrid offspring to develop differently in the womb depending on which species was the father and which was the mother. This pattern has nothing to do with behavior or preference. A similar process in early humans could have made Neanderthal father-H. sapiens mother pairings more likely to produce surviving offspring than the reverse, without either group consciously choosing anything.
"We simply don't know enough yet," Villanea said.
Distinguishing between these explanations — social behavior versus biological incompatibility — will require more Neanderthal genomes from the critical period of contact, ideally spanning multiple geographic regions, experts said.
There's another clue in genetic evidence from a 2026 study of 27 late Neanderthals who lived between 50,000 and 40,000 years ago in what is now Belgium and France. None of those individuals showed any sign of recent ancestry from modern humans, even as H. sapiens from the same era demonstrably carried Neanderthal DNA.
If hybrid children had been raised in Neanderthal groups and went on to reproduce there, those groups' genomes should retain traces of those events — but they don't.
As for whether modern-human groups were patrilocal — with males staying, females moving — the answer is considerably more variable than in Neanderthals. Modern-human communities across cultures show a range of patterns, with both sexes leaving their birth groups depending on circumstance, Alex said. That flexibility may have been part of what made human groups better able to absorb outside individuals.
What we still don't know
Neither genetics nor archaeology has yet been able to answer the question at the center of this story: whether these encounters were by choice, by circumstance, or by force. Platt's team set it aside deliberately, and Alex is careful about it, too.
"We still wouldn't know if it was consensual or coerced," she said.
It's worth being specific about what different scenarios would look like archaeologically. If Neanderthal and modern-human individuals mingled through peaceful alliances, we might expect to find toolmaking techniques or symbolic objects crossing between groups at contact sites — precisely the kind of evidence that is absent at Grotte Mandrin, where, as Slimak noted, the two groups' technical traditions remained entirely distinct.
Slimak, writing from Grotte Mandrin in the middle of his excavation season, urged even more restraint. The genetic data, he said, are "consistent with an asymmetry" — gene flow moved more successfully through Neanderthal males and H. sapiens females than the reverse — but that is where the certainty ends.
The data says nothing about culture, desire, attraction or intent. "That entire social world has been added afterwards," he said.
The same signal, he pointed out, could emerge from a variety of histories — female mobility, demographic imbalance, alliance, exchange, capture, differential survival among hybrids. And these factors could contribute alone or in combination. Even the categories available for describing female movement may be too blunt. A single instance of migration, in traditional societies, can involve marriage, family strategy, alliance, obligation and violence all at once, in combinations that leave no trace for archaeology to disentangle.
Exclusive to Live Science Pro
- 'More Neanderthal than human': How your health may depend on DNA from our long-lost ancestors
- Early Homo sapiens may have lived in rainforests, new clues suggest — and it could overturn our understanding of human evolution
- Scientists show that DNA can last for up to 50,000 years in Africa — much longer than previously thought
"We may identify that a woman came from elsewhere," Slimak said. "We cannot recover her consent."
However, the convergence of genetics, demography and archaeology does reveal a structural picture, if not a sociological one.
The interbreeding was directional and repeated, patterned in ways that map onto the social organization of both groups — and driven in large part, Villanea's model suggests, by the sheer demographic weight of a growing human population folding in what remained of a disappearing one. Neanderthal males, in dwindling and insular communities, appear to have been the ones whose genes crossed into the larger H. sapiens world. Their children, in all likelihood, were raised as humans.
"Genes do not preserve past loves," Slimak said. "They preserve what was transmitted. And between transmission and lived experience lies almost the whole of human society."

Olivia Maule is a former Live Science intern and science journalist whose beats include space, biotechnology and the environment. She holds a B.A. in biology and a B.S. in anthropology from the University of Florida and completed a master's degree in science communication at U.C. Santa Cruz. A 2025 AAAS Mass Media Fellow, she wrote stories and produced videos during a summer at El Nuevo Día, Puerto Rico's largest newspaper, and has written for Eos, Mongabay, Science magazine and Stanford Report. Olivia is a native Spanish and English speaker.

articles.title: Just two drinks a day may be far riskier than you think
articles.text:
Just two drinks a day may be far riskier than you think
- Date:
- October 25, 2026
- Source:
- Journal of Studies on Alcohol and Drugs
- Summary:
- A major new study reveals that drinking just two alcoholic beverages a day is associated with a 1 in 25 lifetime risk of death from alcohol-related causes, challenging the idea that moderate drinking is harmless. Researchers also found no significant overall health benefits from alcohol, with risks rising as consumption increases.
- Share:
Even alcohol consumption that many Americans would describe as moderate may carry significant health risks, including a greater likelihood of premature death, disability, cancer, and heart disease. That is the conclusion of a new study published in the Journal of Studies on Alcohol and Drugs, a journal published at Rutgers University.
The research, known as the Alcohol Intake and Health Study, was originally commissioned by the U.S. federal government to help shape updated national dietary recommendations. Researchers estimated that people who consume an average of 14 alcoholic drinks per week face a 1 in 25 lifetime risk of dying from alcohol-related causes. By comparison, consuming up to seven drinks weekly was linked to only small increases in risk for most health conditions.
"Even low levels of alcohol use come with health risks," says lead study author Kevin Shield, Ph.D., an associate professor at the University of Toronto and a senior scientist who leads the World Health Organization (WHO)/Pan American Health Organization (PAHO) Collaborating Centre in Addiction and Mental Health. "And that risk continues to increase the more someone drinks."
How Scientists Measured the Health Risks of Alcohol
To better understand the long-term consequences of drinking, Shield and his colleagues in the United States and Canada investigated how alcohol consumption over a lifetime contributes to disease and premature death among Americans.
Medical experts first examined more than 7,200 scientific publications covering illnesses and injuries associated with alcohol. Using this evidence, they estimated the risks for individual health conditions and combined those findings with large national health data sets. Statistical models then allowed the team to calculate how different levels of alcohol consumption affect the likelihood of developing serious health problems or dying prematurely.
The findings provide specific estimates that are missing from the latest U.S. Dietary Guidelines. The updated recommendations simply encourage Americans to "limit alcoholic beverages" without identifying a particular consumption threshold. Earlier versions advised men to drink no more than two alcoholic beverages per day and women no more than one.
"While the new U.S. Dietary Guidelines contain a useful 'less-is-best' message, they provide no quantitative framework. Our study was designed to do just that across the drinking spectrum," says study co-author Timothy Naimi, M.D., M.P.H., director of the University of Victoria's Canadian Institute for Substance Use Research and an adjunct professor at Boston University.
"It turns out that two drinks per day, which might be considered 'moderate' from a social standpoint, is associated with a substantially elevated risk of a premature death caused by alcohol," explains Naimi.
Moderate Drinking Offers No Significant Overall Health Benefits
The researchers looked beyond the risk of premature death to examine alcohol's connection to a wide range of immediate and long-term health problems. These included cancers (e.g., esophageal, oral, and breast), cardiovascular disease, liver disease, and injuries.
One of the study's most important findings challenges the longstanding belief that consuming small amounts of alcohol can improve health, particularly heart health.
"We did not observe a significant protective effect of alcohol on health at any level of consumption," says Shield. "At low levels, alcohol may be associated with a reduced risk of ischemic heart disease and stroke. But when you look across the full range of health outcomes, including cancer and other chronic diseases, those potential benefits are outweighed by the risks even at 7 drinks per week."
In other words, while some studies have suggested that light drinking may benefit certain aspects of cardiovascular health, those possible advantages do not translate into an overall health benefit once alcohol's links to cancer and other diseases are taken into account.
Why Individual Alcohol Risks Can Differ
Although the analysis drew on extensive scientific evidence, the researchers emphasize that its estimates describe risks across populations rather than predicting precisely what will happen to any particular person.
Shield says the statistical calculations relied on "the best possible data." However, he cautions that individual circumstances can substantially influence the results.
"However, we can't assume that means one person's individual health risk is the same as what is reported here -- that depends on other factors like lifestyle, genetics, drinking patterns, and other choices that differ person to person."
To estimate alcohol's overall impact, the researchers calculated risks for health conditions already known to be caused by alcohol and combined them into a broader assessment. However, scientists are continuing to investigate additional possible consequences of drinking, including emerging evidence connecting alcohol consumption to pancreatic cancer.
"Understanding those relationships, and how much alcohol contributes to those risks, is an area that still needs further work," says Shield.
What the Findings Mean for U.S. Drinking Guidelines
The results suggest that alcohol-related health risks become more pronounced when consumption exceeds one drink per day, regardless of whether the person is male or female. This provides a more specific reference point for people trying to understand how their drinking habits might affect their long-term health.
Rather than suggesting that any particular amount is completely safe, the findings show how risks increase with greater consumption and why drinking less generally reduces exposure to alcohol-related harm.
"Having a clearer threshold helps people better understand what level of drinking is associated with increased risk and make more informed decisions when drinking," says Shield.
The study has also raised questions about how scientific evidence was incorporated into federal dietary recommendations.
In an accompanying editorial, Robert M. Vincent, a former Associate Administrator for the U.S. Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration, offers his perspective on the circumstances surrounding the research and its role in the development of national guidance.
"The Alcohol Intake and Health report was explicitly invited to inform alcohol guidance during development of the Dietary Guidelines for Americans, 2025-2030," he writes. "Despite the study's adherence to its mandate, its findings were sidelined."

articles.title: Stunning new simulation shows the first galaxies breaking through the Cosmic Dark Age
articles.text:
New simulation of the universe shows the first 2 billion years after the Big Bang play out in stunning detail
A new program aims to help scientists figure out how the ingredients of the universe formed early galaxies, which lit up the cosmos after a "dark age."
Scientists are getting a new glimpse of how the first galaxies came to be. In a stunning new simulation, researchers charted the aftermath of the universe's "dark age," including the appearance of the first galaxies that began to shine about 380,000 years after the Big Bang.
Lumina, the program behind the simulation, catalogs 2 billion years of cosmic time and represents a decent chunk of the 13.8 billion-year-old history of our universe. The results were published Monday (Oct. 26) in the journal Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society.
"Other simulations cannot zoom in as far as this," study co-author Mark Vogelsberger, a professor of physics at MIT, said in a statement. "The difference between the smallest and largest scales that we simulate is larger than in any other simulation."
A video published alongside the paper shows what the scientists saw. The team zoomed in on an area roughly 1.6 billion light-years wide to learn more about how the ingredients of space create galaxies.
Lighting up the Cosmic Dark Age
In the earliest years of our universe, a fog of neutral hydrogen atoms gradually built up, blocking out the light of the first stars. The hydrogen served as a "shroud" and didn't make light visible until galaxies began to form. This ancient, enshrouded period is known as the Cosmic Dark Age.
The video begins in the middle of this epoch, at roughly 45 million years after the Big Bang. Zooming in on one small part of the simulated universe, it slowly reveals a gassy halo giving way to young galaxies shining brightly within it. Included in the calculations are dark matter, stars, gas and radiation — all contributing to the reemergence of cosmic light.
"We see this is where the first galaxies form," first author Oliver Zier, a former postdoctoral researcher and computational astrophysicist at MIT who is now at Harvard University, said in the statement. "And the first stars form in those first galaxies. Those stars then create radiation. The simulation then tracks that radiation, and we can zoom way out to see how that radiation travels out from stars, through the universe, until at some point it ionizes some neutral hydrogen."
Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.
Related stories
Lumina aims to show off two phenomena key to the young universe's history: hydrogen reionization and helium reionization — a first for a program of its kind. Reionization describes how the intergalactic medium, or the area between galaxies, changed from neutral hydrogen to negatively charged ions.
Hydrogen reionization took place when ultraviolet light from young stars and galaxies hit the hydrogen, removing negatively charged electrons from the hydrogen molecules — a process that also allowed light to shine through the fog. Helium reionization happened when supermassive black holes, which have a lot of energy, broke apart neutral helium molecules.
The team said the simulation could eventually be used to validate telescope observations of the early universe, especially those focused on mapping many galaxies at the same time.

Introducing the lumina project: large-volume radiation-hydrodynamic simulations of the epochs of hydrogen and helium reionization. Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society, 552(4). https://doi.org/10.1093/mnras/stag1469
Elizabeth Howell was staff reporter at Space.com between 2022 and 2024 and a regular contributor to Live Science and Space.com between 2012 and 2022. Elizabeth's reporting includes multiple exclusives with the White House, speaking several times with the International Space Station, witnessing five human spaceflight launches on two continents, flying parabolic, working inside a spacesuit, and participating in a simulated Mars mission. Her latest book, "Why Am I Taller?" (ECW Press, 2022) is co-written with astronaut Dave Williams.

articles.title: Three giant black holes discovered in a galaxy from the dawn of time
articles.text:
Three giant black holes discovered in a galaxy from the dawn of time
- Date:
- October 25, 2026
- Source:
- Max Planck Institute for Extraterrestrial Physics, Garching
- Summary:
- Astronomers have discovered three actively feeding black holes inside a single galaxy more than 12.5 billion light-years away, revealing a remarkable scene from the universe’s infancy. Two of the black holes are separated by just 620 light-years and are expected to eventually merge, while a third lurks farther away. One weighs an astonishing 80 million suns, and another is growing faster than conventional theories predict.
- Share:
Astronomers have discovered three actively feeding supermassive black holes in a single galaxy more than 12.5 billion light-years from Earth. The finding, made by an international research team led by the Max Planck Institute for Extraterrestrial Physics (MPE), offers a rare glimpse of how enormous black holes grew and interacted during the universe's earliest stages.
The black holes are located in a galaxy known as J0148-4214. All three are actively accumulating matter, which spirals toward them through surrounding disks of gas and other material. Because the galaxy is so distant, its light has traveled through space for approximately 12.5 billion years before reaching Earth. This means astronomers are observing it as it existed just 1.2 billion years after the Big Bang.
Over such vast distances, the expansion of the universe stretches light to longer, redder wavelengths. Astronomers measure this effect through a property called redshift. For J0148-4214, the researchers measured a redshift of z=5.02, allowing them to determine its remarkable distance.
Three Black Holes in One Ancient Galaxy
"This is the first evidence of three active black holes in a single galaxy in the distant Universe," says Hannah Übler, research group leader at MPE and lead author of the study.
Two of the black holes lie near the galaxy's center, separated by a projected distance of just 620 light-years. The third is much farther out, approximately 5,500 light-years from the center.
The discovery provides important evidence about how massive black holes came together in the young universe.
"It suggests that processes in the early Universe were efficient at bringing massive black holes together, setting the stage for the massive black hole mergers we expect to detect with future gravitational wave observatories," says Übler.
Astronomers believe that galaxy collisions and mergers were common during the universe's early history. As galaxies combined, their central black holes could also move closer together and eventually merge. These mergers would produce increasingly massive black holes at the centers of the newly formed galaxies, potentially helping explain how some grew to enormous sizes so soon after the Big Bang.
How Astronomers Detected the Hidden Black Holes
The researchers identified the three black holes by examining distinctive patterns in the light emitted by hydrogen gas. Near a black hole, powerful gravitational forces cause gas to move at extremely high speeds. These movements leave recognizable signatures in the spectrum of light, allowing astronomers to detect black hole activity even when the objects themselves cannot be seen directly.
In the center of J0148-4214, the team found a particularly complicated hydrogen emission pattern. The best explanation was the presence of two closely spaced black holes rather than a single source.
To distinguish between them, the scientists used a precise measurement technique called spectro-astrometry. By tracking subtle changes in the positions of spectral emissions across the galaxy, they were able to identify the locations of both central black holes, even though the telescope could not resolve them as two separate points of light.
The observations also revealed the third active black hole in the galaxy's outer region.
Three Black Holes With Remarkably Different Masses
The three black holes vary dramatically in size. According to the researchers' calculations, their masses are approximately 80 million, 600,000, and 2 million times that of the Sun.
Surprisingly, the largest black hole is not the one feeding most aggressively. Its smaller neighbor, with a mass of roughly 600,000 suns, is accumulating matter at a much higher rate. In fact, its estimated feeding rate exceeds the maximum predicted by basic models of black hole growth (the Eddington limit).
This unusually rapid growth may offer clues to how some black holes became extraordinarily massive during the relatively short time available in the early universe.
"The JWST data allowed us not only to identify the three black holes, but also to estimate their masses, accretion rates, and the stellar mass of the galaxy," says Dr. Giovanni Mazzolari, second author of the study and researcher at MPE. "We find a total stellar mass of about 1.3 billion suns, and the black holes represent a significant fraction of that."
An Ancient Black Hole Merger in the Making
The two black holes near the galaxy's center are expected to merge within the next few hundred million years. Their eventual collision could help produce an even more massive black hole, illustrating a process that may have been essential to the growth of the universe's earliest cosmic giants.
"These results are extremely exciting," adds Roberto Maiolino, professor at the University of Cambridge and co-author of the study. "They suggest that black hole merging may be an additional, fast route for their rapid growth in the early Universe."
The third black hole presents another intriguing puzzle. Located well outside the galaxy's center, it could be a remnant of an earlier merger that was pushed outward by a powerful gravitational recoil. Such a kick can occur when merging black holes emit gravitational waves unevenly, sending the resulting black hole in the opposite direction.
Another possibility is that the third black hole is gradually moving toward the galaxy's center, where it may eventually interact with the other two.
James Webb Reveals Black Holes That Might Otherwise Remain Hidden
The discovery highlights the remarkable capabilities of the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) for studying black holes in distant galaxies.
In particular, the findings demonstrate the importance of integral field spectroscopy, which allows astronomers to examine how light and its spectral signatures vary across different parts of a galaxy.
Using Webb's Near Infrared Spectrograph in its integral field spectroscopy mode (NIRSpec-IFS), the researchers were able to separate signals that would otherwise have appeared to come from a single black hole.
Without that detailed spatial information, astronomers likely would have identified only one of the galaxy's three active black holes.
The results suggest that other distant galaxies may contain multiple growing black holes that have gone undetected. Finding more of these hidden systems could help scientists reconstruct the history of black hole mergers and better understand how the universe produced its most massive black holes so early in cosmic history.

articles.title: Study reveals new clues to why colorectal cancer in young people is so deadly
articles.text:
Study reveals new clues to why colorectal cancer in young people is so deadly
Colorectal cancer in young people shows genetic and structural differences that may make it more aggressive and treatment-resistant than the cancer tends to be in older people.
Colorectal cancer rates have been rising in people under 50 since the mid-1990s. These early-onset cancers tend to be more aggressive and resistant to treatment than cancers in older adults — and now, scientists may be learning why.
A new study published Thursday (Oct. 29) in the journal Nature Medicine compared colorectal tumors from people between 29 and over 90 years old, and it revealed key differences between young and old patients.
The new findings might, in turn, help scientists uncover new ways to fight colorectal cancer in young people, said study co-author Ana Anderson, a professor of neurology at Harvard Medical School and a core faculty member of the Gene Lay Institute of Immunology and Inflammation at Brigham and Women's Hospital.
"I believe that our study is essentially a turning point now in the field," Anderson told Live Science. "Because up until now, we've had more questions than answers."
Many questions surround early-onset colorectal cancer, as the disease is rising in people under 50 even as it falls in older populations. It's now the leading cause of cancer death in the U.S. for people under 50, and its numbers are even on the rise among children and adolescents.
Beyond questions about what's driving this uptick in cases, another mystery has been why this disease is so deadly in young people.
"The clinical data suggests that the disease in the younger patients is more aggressive overall," Anderson said. "The patients, being very healthy otherwise, do not do well with treatment."
Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.
To investigate that mystery, Anderson collaborated with Dr. Kimmie Ng, an oncologist at the Dana-Farber Cancer Institute, and Dr. Ramnik Xavier, a gastroenterologist at the Broad Institute and Mass General Brigham. They used a method of analyzing RNA in cells that allowed them to work with frozen and banked tumor tissue. RNA, a cousin of DNA, reflects the genes that are active in cells. In all, the team analyzed 189 tumors: 54 from patients under 50 and 135 from patients over 50.
With that many samples, the researchers could look at gradual differences tied to each age group, instead of just comparing tumors between the younger and older groups overall. That enabled them to pinpoint subtle differences, Anderson said.
For starters, younger people had a higher proportion of connective tissue cells in their tumors than they did of malignant cancer cells. That pattern was flipped in patients of older ages. Having a smaller proportion of malignant cells might sound good, but connective tissue in tumors can secrete compounds that suppress the immune system, Anderson said. That helps protect the tumor from immune cells that might otherwise target its cells for destruction.
These connective tissue cells can also physically block chemotherapy drugs from getting to the cancerous cells. This could be one reason younger patients' cancers resist treatment, the researchers suggested.
Based on patterns of gene activity in the tumors, the researchers suspect that younger patients' cancer cells also show distinct activity related to cell-to-cell communication. That may help the cells migrate through the body more easily than cancer cells in older patients do. In other cancers, this kind of gene activity has been linked to more aggressive tumors and a greater chance that the disease will spread, or metastasize, Anderson said.
Related stories
The study's results also turned up an intriguing mystery: the presence of lots of long noncoding RNA. These strands of RNA contain more than 200 building blocks, called nucleotides, that don't provide instructions for building proteins. Coding RNA, in contrast, is ferried to protein-building factories in cells to be used as blueprints.
Scientists don't know what much of this long noncoding RNA does in the body, nor do they understand what it is doing in the tumors specifically. However, they hope to find out.
Anderson and her team are already working on manipulating the RNA they found inside cancer cells in petri dishes. In time, this line of research could supply another piece of the puzzle, helping scientists understand why colorectal cancer is so aggressive in young people.
"It's a new avenue for research into this disease that we previously had no idea about," Anderson said.

Stephanie Pappas is a contributing writer for Live Science, covering topics ranging from geoscience to archaeology to the human brain and behavior. She was previously a senior writer for Live Science but is now a freelancer based in Denver, Colorado, and regularly contributes to Scientific American and The Monitor, the monthly magazine of the American Psychological Association. Stephanie received a bachelor's degree in psychology from the University of South Carolina and a graduate certificate in science communication from the University of California, Santa Cruz.

articles.title: New evidence suggests spinosaurus spent most of its life underwater
articles.text:
New evidence suggests spinosaurus spent most of its life underwater
- Date:
- October 25, 2026
- Source:
- Yale University
- Summary:
- Millions of years after animals first conquered land, some took an extraordinary evolutionary U-turn and returned to the water. Using machine learning and thousands of fossil measurements, Yale scientists have uncovered surprising clues about which prehistoric creatures truly became aquatic. Their findings suggest that Spinosaurus spent most of its life underwater, while some ancient marine reptiles previously thought to be fully aquatic actually spent considerable time on land.
- Share:
For millions of years, evolution helped animals make the transition from life in the ocean to life on land. But the journey did not always move in one direction. Many species eventually returned to the water, developing new adaptations that allowed them to thrive in aquatic environments.
Dozens of major groups of mammals and reptiles made this remarkable evolutionary reversal. Now, a new study from Yale University is shedding light on when and how these transitions occurred, as well as which ancient animals became fully aquatic and which continued to depend on land.
The findings were published in the journal Current Biology.
"These secondarily aquatic groups adapted in strikingly similar ways to their new aquatic home -- evolving flippers and a suite of other features that made them better swimmers," said lead author Caleb Gordon, who completed his doctorate at Yale's Graduate School of Arts and Sciences (GSAS) earlier this year and is now a postdoctoral researcher at the Florida Museum of Natural History. "As a result, they've become textbook examples of convergent evolution, which can tell us a lot about the processes driving and constraining adaptive change in response to similar environmental cues."
Using Ancient Fossils and AI to Reconstruct Evolution
To investigate these evolutionary changes, the researchers examined hundreds of fossil and modern specimens housed at the Yale Peabody Museum and dozens of other institutions worldwide. They collected extensive new data, including measurements (more than 11,000), photographs, and CT scans.
The team combined traditional paleontological techniques with machine learning models that account for evolutionary relationships. They also incorporated a statistical approach originally used by naval forces during World War II. Together, these methods offered a new way to investigate one of the most remarkable transitions in vertebrate evolution.
"Reconstructing the lives of extinct life forms in a scientifically rigorous way, as opposed to just telling stories, is a precise and delicate undertaking," said Bhart-Anjan Bhullar, senior author of the study. Bhullar is an associate professor of Earth and planetary sciences in Yale's Faculty of Arts and Sciences (FAS) and an associate curator of vertebrate paleontology and vertebrate zoology at the Peabody Museum.
"It requires a careful interweaving of data from modern organisms, of which our understanding is necessarily far deeper, and knowledge of these living organisms' genealogy relative to fossil forms," he said. "Caleb's work accomplishes all of this and more, and on a massive evolutionary scale."
For decades, scientists have disagreed about when particular groups of prehistoric animals became fully adapted to life underwater. The fossil record often provides incomplete or conflicting clues, making it difficult to determine whether an extinct species primarily lived on land, in water, or in both environments.
Some skeletal features may indicate an aquatic lifestyle, while others suggest that the same animal remained capable of moving and feeding on land. These contradictions have led researchers to different conclusions about how ancient species behaved.
"In these cases, paleontologists are often stuck, as different lines of evidence disagree about what the ancient animal was like," Gordon said.
To address this uncertainty, Gordon developed a method using relatively simple but effective machine learning models trained on living animals. By identifying relationships between skeletal proportions and known lifestyles, the models can estimate how extinct species used aquatic environments. They can also predict soft tissue adaptations, including swimming structures that rarely survive in fossils.
Spinosaurus May Have Spent Most of Its Life Underwater
One of the most striking findings concerns Spinosaurus, a giant prehistoric dinosaur whose relationship with water has generated considerable controversy.
Spinosaurus lived approximately 113 million to 94 million years ago in what is now northern Africa. Although scientists generally agree that it was associated with aquatic environments, exactly how it moved, hunted, and spent its time remains a subject of debate.
Some evidence points to an animal that frequently submerged itself and pursued prey underwater, much like seals or penguins. Other findings suggest a lifestyle closer to that of a modern heron, with Spinosaurus walking and searching for food along shorelines and in shallow water.
The Yale team's analysis provides new support for the more aquatic interpretation.
"Our results shed new light on how much time Spinosaurus spent submerged, which could support the underwater hunting view," Gordon said. "We confidently recovered highly aquatic habits for Spinosaurus, indicating that it spent the vast majority of its time submerged in the water."
Although the findings do not settle every question about how Spinosaurus hunted, they strengthen the case that this enormous predator spent much more of its life underwater than on land.
Ancient Marine Reptiles That Never Fully Left Land
The researchers reached a different conclusion about mesosaurs, small marine reptiles that lived between 290 million and 274 million years ago in regions now forming parts of South Africa and eastern South America.
Mesosaurs have long interested paleontologists because they gave birth to live young, a characteristic some researchers have interpreted as evidence of a fully aquatic existence. However, the new analysis suggests that their limbs were not adapted for a life spent entirely in water.
Instead, their skeletal proportions indicate that mesosaurs regularly moved between aquatic and terrestrial environments.
"They spent a lot of time on land, like a modern-day alligator or platypus does," Gordon said. "Mesosaurs didn't completely leave the land behind."
The findings also suggest a broader pattern among the earliest marine reptiles. According to the researchers, all Paleozoic marine reptiles (all marine reptiles around before the dinosaurs appeared) continued to return to land regularly. None appeared to have evolved a completely aquatic lifestyle, with even the most water adapted species remaining amphibious.
The researchers found that forelimb proportions were particularly useful for distinguishing these lifestyles. Using this information, their models could predict with more than 90% accuracy whether an animal possessed soft tissue flippers and whether it had highly or fully aquatic habits.
A World War II Technique Helps Solve an Evolutionary Mystery
An especially unusual part of the research involved adapting a statistical method developed during the 1940s.
"Caleb resurrected a statistical technique from a bygone era," said co-author Jacques Gauthier, a professor of Earth and planetary sciences at Yale and curator-in-charge for vertebrate paleontology at the Peabody Museum. "It was developed during WWII to estimate the probability that an approaching blip on the radar screen was an enemy plane. Caleb cleverly used it to get at whether or not an extinct animal had limbs modified for swimming."
By repurposing this approach, the researchers could assess the likelihood that an extinct species possessed specialized swimming adaptations, even when direct evidence of those features was missing.
The method could eventually help scientists investigate other major changes in evolutionary history. Potential applications include studying when human ancestors developed the ability to walk on two legs and how the dinosaur ancestors of birds evolved the ability to fly.
A New Way to Understand Extinct Animals
Because most prehistoric vertebrates are known primarily through their fossilized skeletons, reconstructing their behavior is one of paleontology's greatest challenges. Bones preserve valuable information, but they rarely provide a complete picture of how an animal lived.
Traditionally, scientists have interpreted particular skeletal features to make arguments about the lifestyles of extinct species. Those interpretations can differ significantly, especially when fossils are incomplete or several anatomical characteristics point toward different conclusions.
The new approach offers a more systematic way to evaluate that evidence, using patterns observed in living species to make testable predictions about animals that disappeared millions of years ago.
"Bones are all that is left to us of the vast majority of vertebrate animals that have lived on Earth," Bhullar said. "We want to know so very much about these creatures and the succession of lost worlds they inhabited, but we have so little on which to base our conclusions. From skeletal remains, people have tried to discern life habits, generally making an argument on the basis of one preferred set of features or another. Caleb's method removes the subjectivity from this process and allows the data to speak for themselves."
The study's additional co-authors are Lisa Freisem, a doctoral student at Yale's Graduate School of Arts and Sciences, and Christopher Griffin, an assistant professor of geosciences at Princeton University who previously worked as a postdoctoral fellow at Yale.
Research support was provided by the Yale Institute for Biospheric Studies, the International Union for Conservation of Nature's Crocodile Specialist Group, and the National Science Foundation.

articles.title: Scientists discover how pancreatic cancer rewrites its DNA to escape treatment
articles.text:
Scientists discover how pancreatic cancer rewrites its DNA to escape treatment
- Date:
- October 25, 2026
- Source:
- NYU Langone Health / NYU Grossman School of Medicine
- Summary:
- Scientists have discovered how pancreatic cancer cells continually reshape their genetic makeup to become more aggressive, spread, and evade treatment. In laboratory experiments, blocking a key gene reversed some of these dangerous changes, revealing a potential new way to fight the deadly disease.
- Share:
Scientists have uncovered new details about how pancreatic cancer constantly changes its genetic makeup, allowing it to become more aggressive, spread throughout the body, and resist treatment. By examining nearly half a million individual cancer cells, researchers identified genetic changes that could reveal new ways to fight one of the deadliest forms of cancer.
The study, conducted by scientists at NYU Langone Health and its Perlmutter Cancer Center, focused on pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma, a particularly difficult cancer to treat. Nearly 85 percent of patients die within five years of being diagnosed.
Although researchers have already linked more than half a dozen genes to the disease, much remains unknown about how pancreatic cancer develops and adapts. By examining tumor cells individually rather than studying them in large groups, the team gained a clearer understanding of how different populations of cancer cells change their DNA as the disease progresses.
How Pancreatic Cancer Evolves To Escape Treatment
The researchers discovered that pancreatic tumors contain a variety of distinct cell populations known as clones. Each clone consists of cancer cells with similar genetic characteristics, but their behavior can differ dramatically.
Some clones develop changes that help them withstand cancer treatments, while others become better equipped to invade surrounding tissues and spread to other parts of the body. These findings suggest that the cancer's ability to continually reorganize its genetic material plays a central role in both treatment resistance and metastasis.
Previous studies generally divided pancreatic cancer cells into two main categories: classical (less aggressive) and basal (more aggressive). However, because those studies examined large collections of cells together, scientists could not fully explain how cancer cells move from one category to the other.
The latest findings help explain this process. Genetic changes occurring within individual tumors allow cancer cells to shift between these two states, potentially making the disease more dangerous as it develops.
Scientists Identify a Gene That Could Make Pancreatic Cancer Less Aggressive
Published on October 13 in Nature Genetics, the study identified several genetic changes associated with pancreatic cancer progression. One particularly important finding involved MYC, a gene that showed heightened activity in some of the most aggressive cancer cell populations.
In additional laboratory experiments, the researchers blocked MYC activity in aggressive basal pancreatic cancer cells. Remarkably, the cells shifted back toward the less aggressive classical state.
The change also made the cancer cells more exposed to immune cells, suggesting they could become easier for the immune system to recognize and attack. Although further research is needed, the results point to MYC as a promising target for future pancreatic cancer treatments.
"Our study provides the most granular view to date of pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma, revealing how ongoing genetic reshaping drives tumor evolution over the course of disease," said study lead investigator Despoina Kalfakakou, PhD, a postdoctoral research fellow at NYU Grossman School of Medicine and Perlmutter Cancer Center. "These findings suggest that targeting the mechanisms underlying tumor evolution, including MYC, may help restrain the cancer's rapid progression."
"Our research also suggests that single-cell clonal analysis offers a better approach to understanding complex cancers, like pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma, as it develops over time, by mapping how tumors evolve and adapt at each stage of disease progression," said study co-senior investigator Aristotelis Tsirigos, PhD, a professor in the Departments of Medicine and Pathology at NYU Grossman School of Medicine and a member of Perlmutter Cancer Center.
"More broadly, our study results highlight the critical role of clonal diversity, genetic plasticity, and interactions with the tumor's microenvironment in shaping human pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma biology," said Dr. Tsirigos, who is also co-director of the Division of Precision Medicine and director of NYU Langone's Applied Bioinformatics Laboratories.
Why Pancreatic Cancer Can Evade the Immune System
The investigation also provided important clues about pancreatic cancer's ability to hide from the immune system, a characteristic that may help explain why the disease often responds poorly to immunotherapy.
Researchers discovered that certain cancer cell clones showed increased activity of the TIGIT gene, which is associated with proteins that help tumors escape immune detection.
At the same time, these clones exhibited reduced activity of the PD1 gene. This combination may help explain why immunotherapies designed to target PD1 have shown limited effectiveness against pancreatic cancer.
Understanding these differences between cancer cell populations could help scientists develop treatments that interfere with the specific mechanisms tumors use to avoid immune attack.
According to Dr. Tsirigos, clinical trials investigating drugs that inhibit MYC or TIGIT are already underway for pancreatic ductal carcinoma and other cancers. He said the latest findings underscore the need for larger studies examining the different states cancer cells can adopt and how treatments might be tailored to target them.
Nearly Half a Million Cancer Cells Reveal Hidden Tumor Diversity
To investigate how pancreatic cancer changes over time, the scientists examined gene activity (using transcriptomics) in 443,451 individual cells collected from 62 tumors belonging to 56 men and women diagnosed with pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma.
Six of these patients also provided tumor samples both before and after chemotherapy, allowing researchers to examine changes associated with treatment.
Unlike traditional approaches that measure changes in gene activity across large groups of cells, the new analysis examined individual cells. This provided a much more detailed picture of the different cancer cell populations living within the same tumor.
The results showed that individual tumors contained approximately two to 11 distinct clones, consisting of varying combinations of classical and basal cancer cells.
By tracing the genetic origins of these clones and comparing patterns of gene activity, the researchers connected differences in DNA copy numbers with the types of cells present in each tumor.
This approach allowed them to identify which genes, including MYC and TIGIT, were particularly active at different points during cancer progression.
Together, the findings provide a more detailed understanding of how pancreatic tumors evolve, resist treatment, and spread. They also suggest that interfering with the genetic mechanisms driving these changes could offer new opportunities to combat a disease that remains exceptionally difficult to treat.
Study Funding and Research Team
The research was supported by the Sky Foundation and National Institutes of Health grants P30CA016087 and R01CA245005.
In addition to Drs. Kalfakakou and Tsirigos, the NYU Langone research team included Daniel Cameron, MS; Emily Kawaler, PhD; Ziaohong Jing, PhD; Cristina H. Hajdu, MD; Dylan Tamayo, MS; Yoona Shim; Amanda Ackermann, MD, PhD; Daniel Weissinger; Rosmel Hernandez, PhD; Matthew Beier, MD; Dacia Dimartino, PhD; Peter Meyn; Kalina Rice, MS; Shanmugapriya Selvaraj, MS; Cynthia A. Loomis, MD, PhD; Adriana Heguy, PhD; Amanda W. Lund, PhD; and Igor Dolgalev, PhD.
Additional contributors from Oregon Health and Science University were co-investigators Motoyuki Tsuda, MD, PhD; Hayley Zimny; and Rosalie Sears, PhD.
Researchers from the University of California San Diego included Lidong Wang, PhD; Qi Su, PhD; Sungsik Kim, PhD; Hannah Carter, PhD; Theodore Welling, MD; and co-senior study investigator Diane Simeone, MD.
